surveyDefinition.title: Running Shoes — consumer survey (China)
surveyDefinition.studyPurpose: Identify which of 4 behavioural segments each respondent belongs to, based on running frequency, purchase drivers, fit and durability priorities, and price sensitivity.

segments.name: Performance-Focused Runners
segments.description: Run multiple times per week, prioritise cushioning, support and durability, willing to pay premium for technology and brand trust. They research extensively and replace shoes based on mileage or wear.

segments.name: Value-Seeking Buyers
segments.description: Run or jog occasionally for fitness or commute, buy mid-range shoes, highly price-sensitive, prioritise durability and comfort but switch brands for better value. They replace only when worn out.

segments.name: Style-Driven Users
segments.description: Buy running shoes primarily for casual wear or light activity, driven by aesthetics and brand image, less concerned with technical performance. They own multiple pairs and replace for fashion reasons.

segments.name: Eco-Conscious Users
segments.description: Run regularly and are strongly motivated by sustainability, willing to pay more for eco-friendly materials and ethical brands, even if it means compromising on some performance or style.

surveyDefinition.whatThisSurveyIs: A segmentation study of Running Shoes buyers in China. It asks how people use Running Shoes, how they choose it, and what would make them switch — then sorts respondents into the behavioural groups defined below. Questions stay at category level: no named brands, and nothing about adjacent categories.
surveyDefinition.whoseContextThisIs: Adults in China who buy or use Running Shoes for personal or household use. Respondents qualify if they: Individuals who have bought running shoes in the past 12 months; Individuals who run or exercise regularly (at least once a week); Individuals who are the primary decision-maker for their own shoe purchase. Excluded: Professional athletes whose shoes are provided by sponsors; Businesses purchasing shoes for employees or resale; Children under 18 (unless purchasing for themselves, but typically parent decides).
surveyDefinition.whyTheseRespondents: Everyday consumers buy running shoes for personal use, pay for them out of pocket, and decide which pair to purchase based on fit, style, and performance. While some businesses may purchase shoes for employees (e.g., athletic teams), the dominant and defining buyer is the individual consumer.
respondentBehaviours: Engages in running or jogging at least occasionally
Purchases athletic footwear for fitness, sport, or casual wear
Researches brands, reviews, and features before buying
May be brand loyal or open to switching based on price/performance
whatIsDeliberatelyNotAsked: Age or household income as behavioural questions — no finding in this survey is driven by them. They are asked once, at the end, in Profiling, and used only to cross-tabulate the behavioural results.
Brand, company or manufacturer names — the survey stays at category level so findings are not tied to one competitor set.
Where the respondent lives — region is chosen when viewing the results, so asking it again would waste a question.
surveyDefinition.howToReadTheNumbers: Percentages are modelled estimates built from published market evidence — they are not measurements from fielded interviews, and should be read as an expected shape of response rather than a result. Single-choice, ranking and rating-scale questions sum to 100%. Multi-select questions do not — each option is an independent share of respondents choosing it. The N shown on each question is the display base for that item.

structure.storyline: Questions run in a planned narrative order: broad and easy first, specific and sensitive last.
structure.storylineSummary: The survey opens by establishing the respondent's running habits and shoe ownership, then moves through their purchase journey – from trigger to channel to spend – and finally probes their preferences, trade-offs, and satisfaction. This arc separates the four segments by their running purpose, price sensitivity, and priorities, allowing the client to target each group with tailored messaging and product development.

targetCustomer.summary: Adult consumers of Running Shoes in China — who Individuals who have bought running shoes in the past 12 months; Individuals who run or exercise regularly (at least once a week); Individuals who are the primary decision-maker for their own shoe purchase. The survey targets the end consumer who buys and uses running shoes for personal fitness and lifestyle. This audience represents the primary market for running shoes globally.

questions.question: In a week, how many times do you run?
questions.insight: Top response: 1–2 times a week (38.00%).

questions.question: Where do you run?

metadata.studyPurpose: Identify which of 4 behavioural segments each respondent belongs to, based on running frequency, purchase drivers, fit and durability priorities, and price sensitivity.
metadata.segmentation_lens: Jobs-to-be-done combined with price sensitivity: running shoes are hired for distinct purposes (performance training, daily fitness, casual style, budget necessity) and these purposes drive different purchase behaviours and price trade-offs. This lens separates buyers more meaningfully than usage fr

segments.name: Performance-Focused Runners
segments.description: Run multiple times per week, prioritise cushioning, support and durability, willing to pay premium for technology and brand trust. They research extensively and replace shoes based on mileage or wear.
segments.hypothesis: They will report high frequency, high spend, low price sensitivity, and strong preference for performance features over style.

segments.name: Value-Seeking Buyers
segments.description: Run or jog occasionally for fitness or commute, buy mid-range shoes, highly price-sensitive, prioritise durability and comfort but switch brands for better value. They replace only when worn out.
segments.hypothesis: They will report moderate frequency, mid-range spend, high price sensitivity, and cite price and durability as top decision drivers.

segments.name: Style-Driven Users
segments.description: Buy running shoes primarily for casual wear or light activity, driven by aesthetics and brand image, less concerned with technical performance. They own multiple pairs and replace for fashion reasons.
segments.hypothesis: They will report lower running frequency, moderate spend, and rank style and brand above performance features.

segments.name: Eco-Conscious Users
segments.description: Run regularly and are strongly motivated by sustainability, willing to pay more for eco-friendly materials and ethical brands, even if it means compromising on some performance or style.
segments.hypothesis: They will report high frequency, high spend, low price sensitivity, and prioritise sustainable materials and claims over other attributes.

segmentModel.tie_break: The question 'cp3' (main reason you run) is the most direct behavioural self-report to settle ties, because it explicitly distinguishes training/racing (performance), commuting (value), and fun/casual (style) motivations, while eco-consciousness is better captured by pe5/pe6.
notes: Eco-conscious segment is primarily identified through willingness to pay more for sustainable materials (pe5) and sustainability claims (pe6), plus sf5 and sf4.
Style-driven segment is identified through fashion-driven replacement (cp7, bb1), multiple pairs (cp5), and style priority (sf5).
Value-seeking segment is identified through price sensitivity (bb5, bb6), commuting motivation (cp3, cp4), and durability focus (pe2, sf5).
Performance-focused segment is identified through high frequency (cp1), racing motivation (cp3, cp4), premium price (bb5), and performance priority (bb6).

fieldingNotes.recommendedSample: n=800-1,200 for stable segment-level sub-groups (roughly n>=312 per segment after weighting). At n=1,000 the margin of error on a whole-sample percentage is about ±3.1pp at 95% confidence; on a segment of n=200 it widens to about ±6.9pp, so segment-level differences under ~10pp should not be reported as real.
fieldingNotes.quotaControls: Apply quotas on the category-usage and frequency screeners so heavy users — who are more willing survey-takers — are not over-sampled.
scriptingNotes: Rotate the order of answer options on every non-ordinal question to remove primacy bias. Do NOT rotate ordinal scales (frequency bands, price bands, satisfaction) — their order carries meaning.
Anchor 'Other', 'None of these' and 'Prefer not to say' to the bottom of the list, exempt from rotation.
Every 'Other' option takes an open-text capture, coded back into the frame at analysis if any single verbatim exceeds 3%.
No routing or skip logic: every respondent sees every question, so the base is constant across the instrument.
Include one attention check in the middle third — a standard instructed-response item. Terminate on failure and replace.
Randomise the order of the two ranking/trade-off items between respondents so neither is systematically answered while fresher.
caveats: Percentages in this document are modelled from published market evidence, not measured from fielded interviews. Replace them with primary data once the study is run.
Ranking items are shown as a lighter-weight ranking exercise; run them as MaxDiff if you need more precision on driver importance.
Profiling questions are for cross-tabs only and are excluded from the segmentation scoring model.

metadata.storyline_summary: The survey opens by establishing the respondent's running habits and shoe ownership, then moves through their purchase journey – from trigger to channel to spend – and finally probes their preferences, trade-offs, and satisfaction. This arc separates the four segments by their running purpose, price sensitivity, and priorities, allowing the client to target each group with tailored messaging and product development.
storyline_notes: Replaced generic 'category relationship' with 'running frequency and context' to directly capture engagement level.
Added 'shoe ownership' and 'replacement cycle' beats to reflect the durable nature of running shoes and the importance of replacement behaviour.
In the buying section, added 'price paid' as a distinct beat to capture actual spend, crucial for price sensitivity segmentation.
In preferences, added 'fit and sizing' as a dedicated beat due to the high pain point of online fit issues in the region.
In satisfaction, merged 'satisfaction drivers' into 'comfort and injury problems' to focus on the most actionable unmet needs.
All beats are designed to be answerable with closed questions and avoid demographic or brand-specific questions.
metadata.classification_reason: Everyday consumers buy running shoes for personal use, pay for them out of pocket, and decide which pair to purchase based on fit, style, and performance. While some businesses may purchase shoes for employees (e.g., athletic teams), the dominant and defining buyer is the individual consumer.
